segments.title: Operation Tan No. 2 and decisive-battle thinking
segments.body: Operation Tan No. 2 grew from the Imperial Japanese Navy's expectation that a decisive blow against American carriers could still change the war. This expectation survived repeated setbacks in the Pacific. American submarines were meanwhile cutting Japan's supply lines and making supplies harder to obtain. The plan retained the ambition of a decisive battle while Japan's capacity to fight one continued to shrink.

evidence.note: Japanese decisive-battle expectations and the Pacific strategic situation.
American submarine attacks on shipping, restricted supplies, and repeated doctrinal assumptions.

segments.summary: Operation Tan No. 2 grew from Japan's continuing search for a decisive fleet blow even as its strategic position collapsed.

segments.title: A reconnaissance chain with modern strike-warfare lessons
segments.body: Tan No. 2 depended heavily on reconnaissance to establish the enemy fleet's location. Its kamikaze aircraft can be compared with crewed long-range cruise missiles. That comparison makes the operation relevant to modern strike warfare even though the delivery method differs. A distant target and a complicated plan still require reliable information about where the enemy is.

evidence.note: A comparison between kamikaze aircraft and crewed cruise missiles, with reconnaissance essential to both.

segments.summary: Tan No. 2 illustrates why a long-range strike depends on finding the enemy before launching the attack.

segments.title: From the first Majuro plan to Tan No. 1
segments.body: The earlier Majuro plan called for nine aircraft carriers, four escort carriers, 530 carrier aircraft, and another 300 aircraft from island bases. Five submarines were also to carry ten amphibious light tanks armed with aerial torpedoes, which would cross the coral reef and attack carriers in the anchorage during the air strike. The air component resembled the Philippine Sea battle plan, although this was a separate operation. Mitsuo Fuchida's later Tan No. 1 proposal reduced the attacking force to 27 torpedo bombers and 27 dive bombers, after reconnaissance from Truk. It still aimed at a heavily defended anchorage expected to hold roughly twenty American carriers. A second Pearl Harbor remained the ambition despite the reduction from 830 aircraft to 54.

evidence.note: The earlier Majuro plan's carrier, aircraft, submarine, and amphibious tank forces.
The earlier operation is explicitly distinguished from the Philippine Sea battle.
Fuchida's 54-aircraft plan and the expected concentration of American carriers at Majuro.
A second Pearl Harbor remained the aim despite a force of only 54 aircraft.

segments.summary: The earlier plans show a striking contraction from a carrier-and-land-air offensive to a proposed 54-aircraft raid on Majuro.

segments.title: A successful strike could have delayed Okinawa
segments.body: Tan No. 2 took place shortly before the Okinawa campaign, when British naval forces were becoming a larger presence in the Pacific. A fully successful attack is estimated here to have delayed Okinawa by six or eight months, perhaps as long as a year. That would have bought Japan time and potentially prolonged the war. The estimate still gives Japan no route to victory.

evidence.note: Conditional estimate of a six-to-eight-month Okinawa delay, possibly a year, without Japanese victory.

segments.summary: One estimate gives a fully successful strike enough effect to delay Okinawa for months, while leaving Japan unable to win the war.

segments.title: Escort production separated Britain from Japan in submarine war
segments.body: A comparison between the American submarine campaign against Japanese shipping and the German campaign against Britain exposes the importance of defensive industrial capacity. Britain answered with anti-submarine trawlers, Flower-class corvettes, River-class frigates, Castle-class corvettes, and converted destroyers. Its economy retained rear areas and enough industrial depth to sustain that construction, although a global war stretched those advantages. Japan's weaker escort investment and industrial base left its maritime supply system far more exposed to American submarines.

evidence.note: British escort construction and the industrial demands of a global war.

segments.summary: Britain's escort-building capacity helped it sustain defenses against submarines that Japan's smaller industrial effort could not match.

segments.title: Could Japanese civilians and servicemen see defeat coming?
segments.body: Japanese civilians needed enough geographical knowledge to recognize that the fighting was moving closer to the home islands. Propaganda and information control limited what they knew, while secrecy and contemporary ideas about honor complicated their interpretation of events. Even someone who believed the war was going badly could still believe victory was possible. Recognizing deterioration also did not establish whether that person would act on the belief.

evidence.note: Propaganda, geographical knowledge, secrecy, honor, and the distinction between recognizing setbacks and accepting defeat.

segments.summary: Propaganda, secrecy, and geographical knowledge affected whether Japanese civilians and servicemen recognized how badly the war was going.
segments.question: Was belief in continued victory confined to Japanese high command, or did civilians and servicemen also think the war could still be won?
segments.answerShort: Some probably noticed the shrinking defensive perimeter, but information control and limited geographical knowledge complicated that judgment. Believing the war was going badly did not necessarily mean believing it was lost or acting accordingly.

segments.title: Japanese expectations of British armored carriers
segments.body: British armored carriers had been designed with heavy air attack in mind. Japanese expectations also drew on German and Italian claims that some of those ships had already been sunk. Illustrious, Victorious, and Formidable nevertheless appeared in the Pacific as operational carriers. Their survival exposed the unreliability of repeated Axis sinking claims.

evidence.note: British armored carriers, repeated Axis sinking claims, and the appearance of surviving carriers in the Pacific.

segments.summary: British carriers arrived in the Pacific despite repeated German and Italian claims that they had been sunk.
segments.question: Did Japanese planners understand that British armored carriers were designed to withstand the kinds of attacks being made against them?
segments.answerShort: Not fully, and German and Italian claims to have sunk several British carriers further confused the picture.

segments.title: Factionalism distorts Japanese naval command
segments.body: The Philippine Sea comparison places six Japanese vice admirals and five rear admirals against an American structure of one admiral, two vice admirals, and ten rear admirals. Too many officers at the same senior rank made authority less clear. Rival factions also withheld capable commanders to avoid sharing credit. These command disputes followed Admiral Koga's death in a flying-boat crash and helped frustrate the earlier Majuro plan.

evidence.note: Japanese and American admiral ranks at the Philippine Sea, Koga's death, and factional disputes over commands and credit.

segments.summary: The failure to establish a clean chain of command left too many senior admirals competing for authority and credit.

segments.title: Carrier survivability reflects production scale
segments.body: Carrier survivability cannot be ranked apart from production scale. A navy building only two carriers has strong reason to make each as difficult to sink as possible, while a navy building two dozen can accept different tradeoffs. American designers still valued protection and damage control, but they could also prioritize larger air groups, speed, and construction efficiency because one loss would not remove half the fleet. Fleet size and replacement capacity shaped survivability choices as much as armor did.

evidence.note: Design priorities when building two carriers compared with two dozen.

segments.summary: The design balance between protection, air-group size, speed, and ease of construction changes when a navy can build dozens of carriers instead of two.
segments.question: Had planners forgotten how difficult American carriers were to sink?
segments.answerShort: American carriers had effective damage control, while their balance of protection, air-group size, speed, and ease of construction reflected a fleet built in much larger numbers.

segments.title: Why Japan did not disperse warship construction
segments.body: Singapore had facilities theoretically capable of building ships, particularly escorts. Additional yards could also have been established in Korea. Funding limited what could be done, and the desire to disperse construction was weak. Treating these territories as vassal states and wanting to employ Japanese workers discouraged the expansion.

evidence.note: Potential shipbuilding at Singapore and Korea, limited finance, and the preference for Japanese employment.

segments.summary: Japan had access to facilities elsewhere in its empire but did little to turn them into a distributed naval construction base.
segments.question: Did the Imperial Japanese Navy try to build ships outside the Japanese home islands, especially in resource-rich occupied territories?
segments.answerShort: Not to a significant degree. Singapore could have supported some construction and Korea could have hosted expanded yards, but money, policy, and a preference for employing Japanese workers limited that approach.

segments.title: Japanese radar equipment delayed the supporting submarines
segments.body: Japan had developed its own radar equipment. Some submarines assigned to support Tan No. 2 were delayed while that equipment was fitted. Japanese planners therefore knew about radar, and its installation affected the preparation of their own force.

evidence.note: Japanese radar development and delays while supporting submarines received radar equipment.

segments.summary: Japan possessed radar, and installing it on the supporting submarines delayed their availability.
segments.question: Did Japanese planners understand radar, or did they simply ignore it when designing the attack?
segments.answerShort: They understood radar. Japan had its own equipment, and some supporting submarines were held up while radar was fitted.

segments.title: Who believed Hood was unsinkable?
segments.body: Hood's public reputation should be separated from the Royal Navy's assessment of the ship. Most publicity about an unsinkable Hood did not originate with the navy. The naval assessment treated her as a battlecruiser. If the navy had wanted to advertise an exceptionally protected ship, a battleship such as Nelson or Rodney would have been a more plausible choice.

evidence.note: Popular claims about Hood and the Royal Navy's understanding of battlecruiser protection.

segments.summary: Hood's reputation for invulnerability did not establish that the Royal Navy misunderstood the protection of its battlecruiser.
segments.question: Did the Royal Navy believe its own publicity about an unsinkable Hood?
segments.answerShort: Public belief differed from the navy's professional assessment. Hood was a battlecruiser, and most unsinkability publicity did not originate with the Royal Navy.

segments.title: Why shallow-water torpedo attacks demanded special preparation
segments.body: Tan No. 1 faced the mechanics of attacking ships inside a shallow anchorage. A torpedo bomber could not simply aim at a stationary carrier: the weapon needed space to run, and a steep water entry risked striking the seabed. At Taranto, the Royal Navy had deliberately modified its aerial torpedoes to enter shallow water at a flatter angle. The modifications included an extension wire at the nose to make the torpedo enter with a flatter belly-flop.

evidence.note: Room for torpedoes to run at Majuro and the Royal Navy's shallow-water torpedo preparation for Taranto.

segments.summary: Majuro offered stationary targets, but aerial torpedoes still needed room to run and a controlled water entry; Taranto worked because the Royal Navy had engineered for those constraints.

segments.title: Why one kamikaze could disable Enterprise
segments.body: A single aircraft could achieve an extraordinary result through a pilot's skill. The Enterprise attack is treated as such an exceptional performance. Its success did not establish that a formation of 54 aircraft could repeat the same maneuvers or produce comparable results.

evidence.note: An exceptional individual attack compared with what a 54-aircraft force could be expected to achieve.

segments.summary: The successful attack on Enterprise depended on individual skill that planners could not assume across an entire strike force.
segments.question: How does Tan No. 2 compare with the single kamikaze that knocked USS Enterprise out of the war?
segments.answerShort: The Enterprise attacker displayed exceptional skill, and a maneuver possible for one aircraft could not simply be assumed for a force of 54.

segments.title: Could Swordfish have attacked the anchorage at night?
segments.body: American night air defense still depended heavily on radar-directed gunfire. A slow aircraft such as the Swordfish presented a different problem from the faster aircraft those defenses expected. A hypothetical force of 54 Swordfish is suggested as possibly more effective against the anchorage, with an explicit warning that the idea would need modelling. This was not the Japanese force, and the comparison does not imply that Britain would have chosen Swordfish for such an operation at that stage of the war.

evidence.note: A speculative Swordfish night attack, radar-directed defenses, and the need for modelling before judging its prospects.

segments.summary: A hypothetical Swordfish night strike raises questions about the speed assumptions behind American radar-directed air defense.
segments.question: Were the Japanese planning to use Swordfish for a night attack?
segments.answerShort: No. A hypothetical Swordfish strike might have complicated American radar-directed defenses, but its prospects would need modelling and it was not the Japanese plan.

segments.title: Reconnaissance depends on the Nakajima C6N
segments.body: The Nakajima C6N was a specialist carrier reconnaissance aircraft designed to find the enemy through speed and range. Its single rear-firing machine gun reflected the expectation that it should avoid fighting for information. Carrier service offered advanced equipment and skilled aviation engineers comparable to those at a major home airfield. The aircraft's dependence on that support made it unreliable when the Tan plans required reconnaissance away from its intended operating environment. Failures in the reconnaissance aircraft threatened the operation before the attacking force could begin.

evidence.note: C6N performance, defensive armament, and dependence on skilled maintenance in its intended carrier environment.

segments.summary: The fast C6N reconnaissance aircraft depended on maintenance support that was harder to provide away from its intended carrier environment.

segments.title: Royal Navy experience supports Okinawa's night air defense
segments.body: Royal Navy carriers coordinated airborne night defense around Okinawa. British naval aviation had maintained night operations through much of the war, including continued practice in the Mediterranean. That produced a larger proportion of aircrews experienced in night flying. American dedicated night-fighter carriers concentrated a capability that the Royal Navy maintained more broadly across its carrier force.

evidence.note: British night-flying experience and the contrast with American specialist night carriers.

segments.summary: British carriers helped coordinate night air defense around Okinawa because the Fleet Air Arm maintained a broader pool of crews practiced in night operations.

segments.title: Uncertain protection for C6N fuel tanks
segments.body: Fuel-tank protection was theoretically provided, but its effectiveness is difficult to establish. Japanese production quality was inconsistent. Much knowledge of these aircraft comes from crashed examples. The destruction of design records limits comparison between intended protection and the aircraft actually produced.

evidence.note: Theoretical fuel-tank protection, inconsistent quality control, and missing design records.

segments.summary: The C6N was designed with protective measures for its fuel tanks, but surviving evidence and Japanese quality control make their effectiveness uncertain.
segments.question: Did the Nakajima C6N have self-sealing fuel tanks, or was it highly vulnerable to fire?
segments.answerShort: Protective features were intended, but inconsistent production quality and the loss of Japanese design records make their real effectiveness difficult to establish.

segments.title: Ulithi replaces Majuro as the target
segments.body: Ulithi offered a vast anchorage and room for the facilities needed to support the American fleet. Its position allowed damaged ships to reach support while forcing an enemy to make a substantial effort to attack the base. Much of that support could be brought in afloat, including floating dry docks. Japan's target had changed from Majuro to another extensive anchorage, while the reconnaissance problem remained: the carriers had to be there when the attackers arrived.

evidence.note: Ulithi's anchorage, position, mobile support facilities, and the need to confirm that American carriers were present.

segments.summary: The American move to Ulithi changed the target and required Japanese planners to confirm the carriers' location before a distant attack.

segments.title: Enterprise preservation depended on public support
segments.body: Enterprise is judged to have been in sufficiently good physical condition for preservation, based on accounts of the ship. The obstacle identified here is a lack of support for preserving her. Physical condition and public backing were separate considerations.

evidence.note: Agreement that Enterprise was physically suitable for preservation, qualified by insufficient support.

segments.summary: Enterprise's physical condition is considered adequate for preservation, while insufficient support is identified as the obstacle.

segments.title: Japanese radar ideas outpaced deployment
segments.body: Japanese radar development was more capable than its poor reputation suggests. The larger weakness was getting equipment into widespread service. Industrial capacity limited the scale of production. Radar ideas and designs therefore need to be distinguished from the equipment available to operational forces.

evidence.note: Japanese radar development contrasted with industrial limits on production and deployment.

segments.summary: Japanese radar development faced a production and deployment problem that limited its operational reach.
segments.question: Did Japanese bombers have radar, even if their sets appeared primitive?
segments.answerShort: Japan had radar and ideas for developing it. Limited industrial capacity made widespread production and deployment the larger problem.

segments.title: Ulithi's location makes access valuable
segments.body: Ulithi is identified as part of the Federated States of Micronesia. Its strategic value makes access desirable to a fleet operating in the region. No prediction is given for when an attack would occur.

evidence.note: Micronesian location and the value of access, with no attack-timing forecast.

segments.summary: A question about a possible attack on Ulithi leads to its Micronesian location and the value of access, without a timing prediction.
segments.question: When might China attack Ulithi?
segments.answerShort: No timing forecast is offered. The emphasis is on Ulithi's location in Micronesia and the value of securing access.

segments.title: Why the Royal Navy did not need its own Ulithi
segments.body: British forces could use Ulithi when needed. Their forward support also drew on Australia and the Indian Ocean, whereas American forces were advancing across the Pacific from the opposite direction. Those different approaches affected where each navy needed its support facilities. The Royal Navy consequently did not build an equivalent island base in quite the same form.

evidence.note: British access to Ulithi alongside forward support from Australia and the Indian Ocean.

segments.summary: British forces could use Ulithi, but their Australian and Indian Ocean support network reduced the need to create an equivalent island base.
segments.question: Did the Royal Navy establish an Ulithi-like forward base of its own?
segments.answerShort: Not in the same form; it could use Ulithi when needed and instead relied on forward support from Australia and the Indian Ocean.

segments.title: Ugaki approves Tan No. 2
segments.body: Kamikaze attacks were being promoted as a possible means of winning the war. Tan No. 2 developed in that atmosphere. Vice Admiral Matome Ugaki enthusiastically approved the proposal in early February 1945. The new plan used kamikaze aircraft against the American carrier force.

evidence.note: The perceived promise of kamikaze attacks and Ugaki's approval in early February 1945.

segments.summary: Kamikaze attacks were treated as a potential war-winning weapon when Ugaki approved Tan No. 2 in early February 1945.

segments.title: Reconnaissance losses before the raid
segments.body: Reconnaissance delayed Tan No. 2 before its strike aircraft took off. Of seven C6Ns sent toward Truk in February, two returned to base, one ditched, and another was wrecked on landing. The surviving aircraft reached a base without the spares and servicing support their specialized design needed. By 13 February only one was flyable. Its sortie found no carriers at Ulithi, so even successful navigation and photography could not guarantee a target for the planned attack.

evidence.note: C6N transit losses, missing support at Truk, and the 13 February sortie that found no carriers.

segments.summary: Breakdowns and landing losses reduced seven reconnaissance aircraft to one flyable C6N, which found no carriers at Ulithi.

segments.title: Could Ulithi still support a fleet?
segments.body: Ulithi's usefulness depends partly on support that can travel with the fleet. Floating dry docks are the specific example offered here. A renewed base would bring that infrastructure to the anchorage using the same general approach as the wartime mobile base.

evidence.note: An assessment of Ulithi's usability with floating docks and support brought to the anchorage.

segments.summary: Floating docks could provide support at Ulithi without relying entirely on existing shore facilities.
segments.question: Could Ulithi still be used, and where would its supporting infrastructure come from?
segments.answerShort: Yes. Floating docks and other support facilities could be brought to the anchorage, as they were during the Second World War.

segments.title: Disputed trials of Japanese twin-engine carrier aircraft
segments.body: Reports differ over Japanese tests of twin-engine carrier aircraft. Some accounts say such tests took place, while others dispute them. Neither Japan nor the Royal Navy properly implemented the concept during the war.

evidence.note: Conflicting reports of Japanese tests and the comparison with British development and later implementation.

segments.summary: Accounts of Japanese twin-engine carrier-aircraft tests conflict, and the concept was not properly implemented during the war.
segments.question: Did Japan launch twin-engine aircraft from carriers?
segments.answerShort: There are competing reports about tests, but Japan did not properly implement an operational twin-engine carrier aircraft before the end of the war.

segments.title: A 24-aircraft strike with submarine support
segments.body: The plan combined twenty-four Yokosuka P1Y Ginga bombers with five H8K flying boats for weather reconnaissance and pathfinding. C6Ns would locate the target, while three submarines supplied a radio beacon, aircrew rescue, and logistics. I-58 was assigned the beacon role, Ha-106 the rescue station, and I-366 the supply voyage supporting reconnaissance from Truk. I-366's sixty tons of cargo included thirty-three tons of aviation fuel. The proposed route ran from Japan through storm zones to Ulithi. A small attack force therefore depended on several distant supporting units completing their tasks.

evidence.note: The P1Y strike force, H8K support, C6N reconnaissance, submarine assignments, and route to Ulithi.

segments.summary: Tan No. 2 paired 24 P1Y attack aircraft with flying-boat pathfinders and submarines assigned to navigation, supply, and rescue.

segments.title: Dissent within naval high command
segments.body: The comparison with British command emphasizes officers willing to challenge their colleagues' assumptions. Henderson, Andrew Cunningham, Vian, and Caspar John are offered as examples of people prepared to object forcefully. One account presents Vian's Far Eastern posting as useful partly because his friendship with Mountbatten allowed unusually frank criticism. A story that Vian once punched Mountbatten is treated much more cautiously because it rests on a single source. The proposed command relationship and the doubtful anecdote carry different levels of confidence.

evidence.note: British naval dissent, Vian's reported ability to challenge Mountbatten, and explicit doubt about a single-source fighting anecdote.

segments.summary: Frank criticism within a naval command can restrain overconfident planning, though anecdotes about personal relationships require care.

segments.title: Floating docks offered a higher-value target
segments.body: Ulithi's floating docks offered more operational leverage than another attempt to hit individual carriers. A damaged carrier could be replaced or returned to service, while destroying scarce repair capacity would force damaged ships to travel much farther. That delay would reduce the number of carriers available on station. Maintenance infrastructure could therefore matter more than a prestigious platform.

evidence.note: Scarce floating repair docks as targets with potentially greater operational effect than individual carriers.

segments.summary: Attacking Ulithi's floating repair docks could have constrained carrier availability more effectively than chasing individual hulls.

segments.title: American carrier production exposes the scale mismatch
segments.body: The American carrier programme made a decisive result from twenty-four attackers implausible. Thirty-two Essex-class and six Midway-class carriers were planned or building, with twenty-four Essexes and three Midways ultimately completed in the figures given here. Those totals excluded light and escort carriers. A much larger strike might damage enough ships to delay operations, but even that would buy time rather than change the war's outcome. Decisive-battle doctrine required a force large enough to achieve the result its planners promised.

evidence.note: The twenty-four attackers compared with Essex and Midway construction and completion totals.

segments.summary: A 24-aircraft raid could not decisively affect a navy building dozens of Essex- and Midway-class carriers.

segments.title: Why not use the cargo submarine as a radio beacon?
segments.body: A submarine's ability to carry cargo did not settle its suitability as a radio beacon. The radio equipment needed sufficient electrical power. That requirement constrained which available submarine could perform the role.

evidence.note: Electrical power requirements as a constraint on the submarine assignment.

segments.summary: The beacon role depended on the electrical supply available for radio equipment.
segments.question: Why not use the cargo submarine for the radio-beacon role?
segments.answerShort: The choice depended on which submarines could supply enough electrical power for the radio equipment.

segments.title: Sacrifice without decisive force
segments.body: The twenty-four P1Ys carried seventy-two people whom the mission expected to die. Their deaths were supposed to achieve the victory and honor promised to them. Yet the small attack force offered little chance of producing that result. The ethical criticism concerns commanders committing those lives without giving the crews a credible opportunity to accomplish their mission.

evidence.note: The ethical objection to sacrificing seventy-two aircrew without sufficient force to achieve the promised result.

segments.summary: The criticism of Tan No. 2 is ethical as well as operational: planners committed 72 aircrew without assembling a force capable of earning the promised result.

segments.title: Why Japan kept targeting carriers instead of logistics
segments.body: Japanese officers considered attacks on tankers and other logistics targets but struggled to put those ideas into practice. Doctrine and exercises remained focused on a climactic battle against the enemy's main fleet. That expectation kept pulling target selection back toward fleet carriers. Tan No. 2 continued this pattern despite the importance of the supply and repair ships supporting the American fleet.

evidence.note: Difficulties implementing attacks on logistics and a continuing fixation on the climactic fleet battle.

segments.summary: Decisive-battle thinking drew Japanese attention toward fleet carriers even when tankers and repair capacity offered greater operational leverage.
segments.question: Why did the Imperial Japanese Navy focus on fleet carriers rather than attacking tankers and other logistics ships?
segments.answerShort: Japanese officers considered logistics targets but struggled to implement that strategy, while doctrine and exercises kept pulling attention back to the climactic fleet battle.

segments.title: Why the H8K Emily suited the pathfinder role
segments.body: The Kawanishi H8K Emily combined long range with extensive defensive armament. Its cannon and machine guns invited comparison with the heavily armed Short Sunderland. The range quoted for the aircraft in this operation, 3,888 nautical miles, suggests that early H8K1s may have been used instead of the slightly shorter-ranged H8K2. That identification remains an inference from the published figures. Selecting the longer-ranged aircraft would have improved the prospect of completing the outward journey and returning.

evidence.note: H8K armament and range, with a tentative inference that the longer-ranged early variant was used.

segments.summary: The H8K Emily's armament and long range suited the pathfinder role; the range figures suggest, without establishing, which variant was used.

segments.title: Concentrating kamikaze forces could have raised Allied losses
segments.body: Concentrating kamikaze aircraft and allowing pilots to choose their targets could have made the attacks considerably more dangerous. The expected consequence is substantially greater losses among Allied shipping. This is a counterfactual estimate of the effect of concentration and target choice, with no numerical loss forecast.

evidence.note: Potentially heavier Allied shipping losses from concentration and freer target selection.

segments.summary: A concentrated special-attack force with freedom to choose targets would have posed a greater threat than dispersed small raids.
segments.question: What if Japan had concentrated its kamikaze aircraft in one effort and given pilots freedom to select targets?
segments.answerShort: It could have been considerably more dangerous and might have inflicted much heavier losses on Allied shipping.

segments.title: Submarine logistics and unreliable reconnaissance
segments.body: I-366 carried sixty tons of cargo, including aviation fuel, to support the reconnaissance detachment at Truk. The submarine carried Type 13 air-search and Type 22 surface-search radar. A defective shortwave antenna forced an early return for repair. On the renewed voyage, thirty-foot waves flooded the diesels and swept away deck cargo. Enemy air activity also delayed entry to Truk and unloading. The delivery supplied the material and fuel needed by the only flyable C6N, but its reconnaissance found Ulithi without carriers and the attack was postponed.

evidence.note: I-366's cargo, antenna failure, storm damage, delayed unloading, and reconnaissance postponement.

segments.summary: Antenna failure, severe weather, and enemy air activity delayed I-366's delivery to the vulnerable reconnaissance detachment at Truk.

segments.title: Submarine weather reports and essential cargo
segments.body: Reporting weather was part of the submarines' work even while they carried cargo. The cargo supplied spares and fuel for the reconnaissance aircraft. Without those supplies, the only flyable C6N could not have been kept flying.

evidence.note: Submarine weather reporting and the C6N's dependence on delivered spares and fuel.

segments.summary: The submarines supplied weather information while delivering material essential to C6N reconnaissance.
segments.question: Were the submarines reporting storms while carrying supplies on deck?
segments.answerShort: Yes. Weather reporting was part of their role, and the spares and fuel they carried were essential to keeping the reconnaissance aircraft flying.

segments.title: March reconnaissance fixes the attack date
segments.body: A C6N photographed sixteen carriers at Ulithi on 5 March. Another sortie on 9 March reported carriers in the anchorage and a further group approaching the atoll. Three P-38s intercepted the returning aircraft, which narrowly escaped. Losing it would have removed the remaining reconnaissance capability on which the operation depended. Analysis of its photographs led to 11 March being designated as the attack date.

evidence.note: The 5 and 9 March sightings, escape from three P-38s, and decision to attack on 11 March.

segments.summary: March reconnaissance finally found carriers at Ulithi, but losing the surviving C6N would have ended the reconnaissance effort.

segments.title: I-58 is diverted from an imminent Iwo Jima attack
segments.body: I-58 was about ninety minutes from its kaiten launch position against the Iwo Jima invasion fleet when it was recalled for Tan No. 2. Hashimoto asked to complete the attack first, but the recall stood because no other submarine was available for the required role. Two kaiten were discarded so I-58 could proceed at full speed. The return involved extensive surface running and concern about reefs. Completing the original attack was estimated to delay its arrival by only three to three and a half hours, making the cancellation a substantial opportunity cost of the new assignment.

evidence.note: I-58 was recalled ninety minutes before a planned kaiten attack; Hashimoto asked to continue, but the order stood, and the crew discarded two kaiten so the submarine could serve as Tan No. 2's radio beacon.

segments.summary: Supporting Tan No. 2 pulled I-58 away from a kaiten attack only ninety minutes before its planned launch.

segments.title: I-366 carried C6N spares and fuel
segments.body: I-366's cargo supported the C6N reconnaissance effort. It included spare parts, special fuel, and ordinary aviation fuel.

evidence.note: Confirmation of C6N spares, special fuel, and ordinary aviation fuel aboard I-366.

segments.summary: The supply submarine carried several kinds of material for the reconnaissance aircraft.
segments.question: Did I-366 carry spares for the C6Ns?
segments.answerShort: Yes, together with special fuel and ordinary aviation fuel.

segments.title: The strike disintegrates before Ulithi
segments.body: The strike launched on 11 March 1945 after the pathfinders had already been delayed. Ugaki's briefing allowed crews to return if success appeared unlikely. Five P1Ys turned back with engine trouble, three crashed, and further aircraft were forced back or ditched. Four crash-landed at Yap, possibly because of recently installed radio altimeters. Storm diversions increased the distance flown and consumed fuel from aircraft already operating near their maximum range. Only two P1Ys reached Ulithi to make an attack.

evidence.note: Launch instructions allowing return, delayed pathfinders, mechanical and weather losses, and two arrivals at Ulithi.

segments.summary: Engine failures, crashes, weather, and navigation losses reduced the 24-aircraft force to only two arrivals at Ulithi.

segments.title: Randolph is hit, while the second aircraft crashes on Mogmog
segments.body: The surviving attackers approached after dark, dropped chaff, and came in low over the water. One struck USS Randolph. The other crashed on Mogmog Island beside a lighted baseball diamond, with accounts differing over whether the crew mistook the diamond or its access road for a carrier. No American servicemen were killed on the island, although several American servicemen were injured by debris and burning fuel.

evidence.note: The hit on Randolph and the crash near Mogmog's baseball diamond, with uncertain target identification and injuries on the island.

segments.summary: One P1Y struck USS Randolph; the other crashed beside a lighted baseball diamond on Mogmog Island, possibly after mistaking the diamond or its access road for a carrier.

segments.title: Rapid repair limits the operational effect
segments.body: American losses were 26 dead and 105 wounded. Randolph retained much of her air group despite a hole in the stern. Maintenance ships at Ulithi repaired the carrier in about three weeks, and she returned to action about four weeks after the attack. She served in the Okinawa campaign and later carried the task-force commander's flag after kamikaze attacks disabled Bunker Hill and Enterprise. Forward repairs restored the damaged carrier while American operations continued.

evidence.note: Randolph's damage, casualties, repair, and return to Okinawa.

segments.summary: Ulithi's repair capacity returned USS Randolph to service for Okinawa within weeks, limiting the strike's strategic effect.

segments.title: Which repair ship was alongside Randolph?
segments.body: The ship in the photograph being discussed may be Vulcan. Similar vessels make identification difficult, and some photograph captions disagree. The proposed identification remains uncertain.

evidence.note: Tentative Vulcan identification and conflicting photograph captions.

segments.summary: Conflicting photograph captions prevent a firm identification of the repair ship alongside Randolph.
segments.question: Is the ship alongside Randolph USS Vulcan (AR-5)?
segments.answerShort: Possibly, but the identification is uncertain because some photograph captions disagree.

segments.title: A proposed Dardanelles assault illustrates the need for sufficient force
segments.body: A proposed alternative at the Dardanelles would send ships fitted with false bows, sealed forward compartments, and bulges through the defenses. Troops would follow them toward Constantinople for a landing. The proposal assumes that sufficient protection and a determined advance could force a passage. The comparison with Ulithi concerns the strength committed: attacking a defended target with too little force can reveal an intention without achieving it.

evidence.note: A proposed protected-ship assault at the Dardanelles used as an analogy for concentrating sufficient force at Ulithi.

segments.summary: A counterfactual Dardanelles assault contrasts a concentrated attack with an operation too weak to achieve its objective.

segments.title: Why Tan No. 2 was a Japanese defeat
segments.body: An inconclusive verdict is rejected because the operation caused temporary damage to one American carrier without sinking it. Randolph was back in service within weeks. Japan lost 13 aircraft and roughly 60 to 70 personnel, with most deaths attributed to weather and mechanical failure. Those losses, set against the carrier's rapid return, support the assessment of a Japanese defeat.

evidence.note: Aircraft and personnel losses, the predominance of weather and mechanical causes, and temporary American carrier damage.

segments.summary: Calling the result inconclusive obscures the operational balance: Randolph returned quickly, while Japan lost scarce aircraft and crews largely to weather and mechanical failure.

segments.title: The crews endured an eleven-hour flight to Ulithi
segments.body: Takeoff was at about 09:00, and arrival was at about 20:00. The crews of the aircraft that reached Ulithi had therefore been flying for roughly eleven hours. Their attack came at the end of that long flight and after dark.

evidence.note: An eleven-hour flight calculated from 09:00 takeoff to about 20:00 arrival.

segments.summary: The surviving P1Y crews had been airborne for roughly eleven hours before attempting their night attack.
segments.question: How long had the Japanese crews been flying before they reached Ulithi?
segments.answerShort: About eleven hours, from a 09:00 takeoff to an arrival around 20:00.

segments.title: What would losing fifteen American carriers have changed?
segments.body: Roughly fifteen carriers remained at the anchorage. Sinking all fifteen would have affected American operations and caused some delay. The estimate is that the delay probably would not have been very large. Achieving even that result would first have required an attacking force capable of sinking fifteen carriers.

evidence.note: The hypothetical destruction of fifteen remaining carriers and an estimated limited delay to American operations.

segments.summary: Even with some American carriers withdrawn, sinking the remaining fifteen would have delayed operations, though probably only to a limited extent.
segments.question: What difference did the withdrawal of some American carriers make to the operation?
segments.answerShort: A substantial carrier force remained. Sinking all fifteen carriers cited in the response would have delayed American operations, although the delay was judged unlikely to last very long.

segments.title: Truk was the C6N reconnaissance base
segments.body: The operating base matters to the range comparison. The Tan operation used Truk, so a range comparison based on Tokyo does not describe the mission under discussion.

evidence.note: Truk identified as the reconnaissance base in response to a comparison involving Tokyo and a drop tank.

segments.summary: The relevant C6N mission operated from Truk, which changes a range comparison based on Tokyo.
segments.question: What about the C6N's range from Tokyo with a drop tank?
segments.answerShort: The reconnaissance aircraft for this operation were operating from Truk, not Tokyo.

segments.title: Why Operation Tan No. 2 failed
segments.body: Japanese accounts attributed Tan No. 2's failure to unreliable aircraft engines and the distance the strike aircraft had to fly. Ten P1Y aircrew survived the raid. The operation followed two abandoned plans: an earlier large attack scheme and then Tan No. 1. The move of the American fleet to Ulithi prevented the first Tan plan from going ahead, and Tan No. 2 became the only one of these proposals actually carried out. The closing criticism is that feasibility alone did not provide a good reason to launch it.

evidence.note: Official engine and distance explanations, surviving aircrew, and the progression through abandoned plans to Tan No. 2.

segments.summary: Engine failures and excessive distance undermined the raid, while successive abandoned plans left Tan No. 2 as the attack actually carried out.

segments.title: A kamikaze hit reinforced Enterprise's reputation
segments.body: Putting Enterprise out of action had a morale effect, but the carrier survived. That survival also strengthened her reputation. The distinction in this answer is between disabling a famous ship and actually sinking her.

evidence.note: The morale effect of disabling Enterprise and the reputation strengthened by her survival.

segments.summary: The hit put Enterprise out of action, while her survival strengthened the carrier's reputation.
segments.question: What was the morale effect of the kamikaze hit that put Enterprise out of action?
segments.answerShort: Putting Enterprise out of action had a morale effect, but her survival also strengthened her reputation.

segments.title: Royal Navy propellant remained improved cordite
segments.body: The Royal Navy continued to use cordite after the First World War, with improved formulations. Cordite SC entered use from 1927. Flashless Cordite NF was used during the Second World War. The change was therefore to later grades of cordite rather than a wholly different propellant.

evidence.note: Later cordite formulations, including SC from 1927 and flashless NF during the Second World War.

segments.summary: Interwar rebuilt British capital ships continued to use improved cordite formulations, including flashless types.
segments.question: What replaced cordite in Royal Navy battleships and battlecruisers rebuilt after the First World War?
segments.answerShort: Other, improved grades of cordite rather than a wholly different propellant; SC appeared from 1927 and flashless Cordite NF was used during the Second World War.

segments.title: A heavily armed convoy escort depends on the war
segments.body: The proposed Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts design carries seventy-five four-inch guns and eight torpedo tubes on about 9,000 tons. Its usefulness depends on the war in which it is meant to serve. Four-inch guns could be useful for First World War convoy work or early Second World War anti-aircraft duties. In a Second World War setting, it would look more like an anti-aircraft cruiser, preferably with larger general-purpose weapons around 4.5 or 5 inches. It would probably spend little time accompanying convoys unless it was particularly slow.

evidence.note: A proposed game design assessed against First World War convoy work and Second World War anti-aircraft requirements.

segments.summary: A 9,000-ton escort with many four-inch guns fits First World War convoy needs better than the dual-purpose demands of the Second World War.
segments.question: Would a 9,000-ton convoy-escort cruiser carrying seventy-five four-inch guns and eight torpedo tubes have been useful?
segments.answerShort: Potentially in the First World War or for early anti-aircraft work. For the Second World War, it would be more useful as an anti-aircraft cruiser with larger general-purpose guns around 4.5 to 5 inches.

segments.title: Operating a Westland Wyvern from an escort carrier
segments.body: Operating a Wyvern from an escort carrier was theoretically possible. It would require substantial work on both the carrier and the aircraft. Rocket-assisted takeoff, as used with the Swordfish, is suggested as a probable part of the adaptation.

evidence.note: Theoretical Wyvern operations requiring modifications, probably including rocket assistance.

segments.summary: A Wyvern could theoretically use an escort carrier, but only after substantial adaptation to both aircraft and ship.
segments.question: Could the Westland Wyvern have operated from an escort aircraft carrier?
segments.answerShort: Theoretically yes, probably with rocket-assisted takeoff and significant modifications to the aircraft and carrier.

segments.title: Flashless cordite and The Battle of the River Plate film
segments.body: Flashless cordite is thought likely to have been used in the real battle. Its use in the filming is rejected. The historical comparison remains tentative.

evidence.note: Film propellant distinguished from a tentative historical comparison.

segments.summary: The film did not use flashless cordite; its use in the historical battle is considered likely but remains uncertain.
segments.question: Was flashless cordite used in filming The Battle of the River Plate?
segments.answerShort: No. Flashless cordite was thought likely in the real battle, but not in the filming.

segments.title: Flashless cordite and the size of the charge
segments.body: Flashless propellant reduced the risk of revealing a ship's position during night firing. A slightly lower energy per unit could be offset by increasing the charge. That compensation had physical limits because more propellant occupied more space in the gun. The one-percent reduction is an illustrative example, rather than a measured specification for a named cordite grade.

evidence.note: Illustrative tradeoff between flashlessness, energy per unit, charge size, and space in the gun.

segments.summary: The benefit of flashless firing could justify a modest reduction in energy per unit, provided a larger charge fitted the gun.
segments.question: Was the newer flashless cordite as energetic?
segments.answerShort: A modest reduction in energy per unit could be accepted to avoid revealing a ship at night, with a larger charge compensating where gun dimensions allowed it.

segments.title: How might Tan No. 2 have fared against armored carriers?
segments.body: A comparable attack on a British armored hangar carrier is judged unlikely to cause much damage. Randolph's damage provides the comparison with an unarmored hangar carrier. A hit aft could still have had an effect, so the prediction is qualified by where the aircraft struck.

evidence.note: Randolph's damage compared with the expected effect on an armored hangar carrier, including a caveat about a hit aft.

segments.summary: The expectation is little damage to an armored hangar carrier from a comparable hit, with some allowance for an impact aft.
segments.question: How would Tan No. 2 have fared against Royal Navy armored carriers?
segments.answerShort: Probably little damage, though an impact aft could still have had an effect.

segments.title: Why the cordite yield comparison remains unanswered
segments.body: Explosive yields are normally compared through TNT equivalence. Comparing 112 tons of cordite with a nuclear explosion would first require a suitable conversion into TNT equivalent. No reliable numerical answer is given because that conversion needs further research.

evidence.note: TNT equivalence identified as the necessary comparison, with a numerical answer deferred.

segments.summary: A comparison with nuclear yield requires a TNT-equivalent calculation that is left unresolved.
segments.question: What nuclear-explosion yield would be equivalent to 112 tons of cordite?
segments.answerShort: No reliable figure is given. The cordite first has to be converted into TNT equivalent, and the calculation needs further research.

segments.title: Tentative estimates of cordite stocks and British production
segments.body: An offhand estimate puts a battleship's cordite in the low thousands of tons when charges for all its guns are included. The estimate includes propellant for smaller guns as well as the main battery. British annual production before the First World War is first estimated at 6,000 to 8,000 tons, then corrected to roughly 7,500 to 9,500 tons, with capacity around 13,000 tons. These are offhand figures recalled with a correction during the answer. D-Day is also cited as an operation that reduced Britain's cordite stocks.

evidence.note: Offhand shipboard estimate, corrected British production figures, and wartime stock depletion.

segments.summary: Shipboard quantities and British production are estimated from memory, with a correction to the annual production figures.
segments.question: Could a ship carry thousands of tons of cordite?
segments.answerShort: An offhand estimate suggests low thousands of tons for a battleship when charges for all its guns are included. The figures are recalled from memory, with a correction during the answer.
